title: Carving faces in wood
subtitle: How to carve a stylised face or spirit using stop cuts and chip cuts
excerpt: Carved faces and wood spirits appear on walking sticks and spoon handles, branch ends and relief panels. The technique builds on stop cuts and chip cuts to create the illusion of eyes and brow in a small area of wood. This guide covers the cut sequence and the grain reading that make or break the result.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the chip-cut face method; Carpentry for Boys (1914) for the proportions and relief depth guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A short vertical cut into the wood that sets the boundary before relief cuts, preventing the grain from tearing past the intended line.
Three or more cuts converging to lift a small triangular chip from the surface. The chip-carving fundamental, used for eye recesses in face carving.
A short straight-bladed knife with a stout handle; the standard whittling knife.

content.text: A carved face in a piece of wood works because the eye reads depth that isn't there. Three well-placed chip cuts for the eye recesses, a ridge left standing for the nose, and an undercut at the brow are enough to read as a face from arm's length. The technique is the same whether you are carving a small spirit face on a walking-stick handle or a larger relief on a flat panel. The proportions are fixed and the cut sequence is determined, learn these first and the carving follows.
When to use this technique

Whenever a carved face is required on a handle, a branch end, a flat panel, or a round form. The same cut sequence applies at scales from 2 cm (a spoon handle detail) to 15 cm (a small panel). Works on both green and seasoned wood, though green lime or green sycamore gives the cleanest chip cuts at small scale.
What you need
A
sloyd knife

for the main relief cuts and a detail knife for the eye chips and fine brow work. Both edges must be properly sharp, the chip cut for the eye recess relies on three cuts meeting cleanly at a point, which is only possible with a keen edge. Lime, sycamore, and basswood are best for first attempts; oak and ash work but need more force.
Proportions

On a face area 5 cm tall: the brow ridge sits at 40% from the top; the eyes are 50% from the top, evenly spaced; the nose tip is 65% from the top; the mouth (if carved) is 80% from the top. At any scale, these ratios hold. Divide the face area into thirds: top third is forehead, middle third is nose zone, lower third is mouth and chin.
The cut sequence
1. Mark the face area
Pencil the face area and mark the brow line, eye positions, and mouth line. These marks are guides only, carving adjusts as material comes away.
2. Cut the brow shadow
Make a
stop cut

along the brow line, a firm downward cut 2, 3 mm into the wood. Then make a sloping cut from 5 mm above the brow line down to meet the stop cut, lifting a thin wedge chip. This creates a shadow below the brow ridge that reads as depth at the eye level.
3. Chip-cut the eye recesses

For each eye, use the detail knife to make three cuts converging to a point: first a stop cut along the top of the eye recess (the lower edge of the brow shadow), then two angled cuts from above-left and above-right to meet the stop cut and lift a small triangular chip. This is the
chip cut

. The depth of the chip determines how deeply the eye appears to sit, 2 mm is enough at the 5 cm scale. The grain runs across the face from ear to ear on most round-section blanks: watch the grain direction at the eye chips and ensure the angled cuts go with the grain or the chip lifts ragged.
4. Define the nose ridge

The nose is formed by cutting material away on both sides of the nose centreline, leaving the nose ridge standing proud. Make stop cuts along each side of the nose, then angled cuts from each cheek meeting the stop cuts to lift thin wedges. The nostril flare at the base of the nose is a single small chip cut on each side.
5. Undercut for depth

A slight undercut below the brow overhang, cutting the face surface back 1 mm under the brow stop cut, deepens the shadow at the eyes dramatically. Do this carefully with the detail knife, blade angled back under the brow, taking only a thin shaving. This is the cut most likely to cause the brow to snap if the blank is thin; keep the cut very light.
What a correct face looks like

From arm's length, the face should read as two distinct zones: a shadowed eye zone under the brow and a recessed area either side of the nose. The eyes look like they are set back even though the eye area is only 2 mm deeper than the surrounding surface. Direct overhead light confirms this, the brow casts a shadow over the eye chip if the geometry is right.
Common mistakes
Making the eye chips too deep: a 4 mm eye chip at 5 cm scale looks hollow and skull-like. Keep chips shallow, 1.5, 2 mm.
Skipping the stop cut before the chip cut: without the stop cut boundary, the chip cuts tear past the intended line.
Over-defining the mouth: a spirit face works better with a suggested mouth (a light undercut fold) than a carved set of lips.
